extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of moral philosophy; statesmen and lawgivers interested in ethics
extracted.subtask_description: Exposition of Aristotle's account of the Chief Good (Happiness/eudaimonia), the function of man, and the nature and acquisition of moral and intellectual virtues. Intended to guide both theoretical understanding and practical habituation toward virtuous activity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of the Chief Good / End
rubrics_metrics.description: The Chief Good is 'that for the sake of which the other things are done' — the end or object of pursuit toward which actions aim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: in healing the end is health, in military art victory, in house-building a house. Use the notion of 'for the sake of which' to identify ends; trace instrumentally-related goals back to their ultimate object.

rubrics_metrics.name: Finality and 'Absolutely Final' ends
rubrics_metrics.description: An end is more final if it is pursued for its own sake rather than as a means; 'absolutely final' denotes something chosen always in itself and never for the sake of something else.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determine whether candidate goods are chosen solely for themselves (final) or as instruments for something further (means). If multiple final ends exist, the most final (ultimate) is the Chief Good.

rubrics_metrics.name: Happiness as the final, self-sufficient good
rubrics_metrics.description: Happiness (eudaimonia) is manifestly thought to be final and self-sufficient — chosen always for its own sake and never as a means to something else.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the property of being chosen for itself and being self-sufficient (making life choice-worthy and 'in want of nothing') to test whether a candidate is the Chief Good.

rubrics_metrics.name: Self-sufficiency defined for the final good
rubrics_metrics.description: Self-sufficiency is 'that which taken alone makes life choice-worthy, and to be in want of nothing.' It is not merely solitary individual sufficiency but includes those proper relations (parents, children, friends, countrymen) necessary for a human life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether a proposed good, when present, renders life worth choosing without needing additions; consider reasonable social relations but avoid unlimited extension (friends' friends).

rubrics_metrics.name: Function argument — the work/ function of Man
rubrics_metrics.description: To determine the Chief Good we should discover the work (ergon) of man: if the function of man is 'a working of the soul in accordance with reason', then the human good is activity of the soul in accordance with excellence (virtue).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify what is peculiar to humans (rational activity) and infer the corresponding excellence: as the harp-player's good is to play the harp well, the good of man is to perform rational activity well.

rubrics_metrics.name: Activity in accordance with excellence (virtue) over a complete life
rubrics_metrics.description: Happiness is 'a working of the soul in the way of Excellence,' and it must be exercised 'in a complete life' (εν βιῳ τελείῳ) — not a momentary state but durable activity over time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate lives by sustained virtuous activity, not isolated acts; consider long-term patterns and completeness of life when judging happiness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Happiness as activity, not mere possession
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a crucial difference between conceiving the Chief Good as possession (a state/habit) and as use (activity): the working (activity) cannot be idle, whereas a state might exist without effect (e.g., a sleeping virtuous person).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favor assessments that emphasize active realization of virtue (doing) rather than merely having the disposition; when judging individuals, prioritize exercised virtues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relation of pleasure to happiness
rubrics_metrics.description: Pleasure accompanies virtuous activity for the virtuous person; pleasurable feeling is a mental sensation that is pleasant to the one fond of the corresponding excellence, so pleasure is not merely an appendage but coexists with best acts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating happiness, recognize that true pleasure is integrated with virtuous action for the virtuous agent; beware of treating pleasure as the primary good apart from virtue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement of some external goods
rubrics_metrics.description: Although happiness is primarily activity of the soul, external goods (friends, money, political influence, good birth, children, beauty) are needed in some degree to enable noble actions and complete blessedness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not dismiss external conditions: assess whether an individual has sufficient external instruments to perform noble acts; consider their enabling role without reducing happiness to mere external prosperity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Eligibility: rational activity distinguishes human happiness
rubrics_metrics.description: Non-rational beings (ox, horse) and children (due to tender age) are not properly called happy because they cannot partake in the rational activities that constitute happiness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use capacity for rational action as a criterion for ascribing true happiness; avoid anthropomorphizing animals or prematurely assigning happiness to children who cannot perform rational activity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Completeness and stability of life for happiness
rubrics_metrics.description: To constitute Happiness there must be complete virtue and a complete life; transient success or later ruin (e.g., Priam) prevents one from being rightly called happy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge happiness over the whole course of life: isolated episodes, even long ones, do not suffice if the life as a whole is not complete and stable in virtuous activity.

rubrics_metrics.name: The impact of great misfortune
rubrics_metrics.description: Small changes of fortune do not overthrow happiness, but great and numerous misfortunes can bruise or maim blessedness and prevent or destroy the capacity to act nobly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Differentiate between trivial adverse events and substantial misfortunes when evaluating whether a life remains happy; consider the severity and cumulative effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Happiness as 'precious' and 'final' rather than merely praise-worthy
rubrics_metrics.description: Praise applies to virtues as means to noble acts; Happiness is of a higher class — precious and divine — and serves as the ultimate starting-point or standard to which other goods are referred.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When categorizing goods, reserve 'praise' for virtues and treat happiness as the ultimate evaluative standard or encomiastic target.

rubrics_metrics.name: Division of Excellence: Intellectual vs Moral
rubrics_metrics.description: Human Excellence (virtue) is of two kinds: Intellectual (pure science, intelligence, practical wisdom) — arising mostly from teaching, experience and time — and Moral (liberality, self-mastery) — arising from habit/custom.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish virtues by their source in evaluation or formation efforts: design pedagogy for intellectual virtues (teaching, time, experience) and habituation/legislation for moral virtues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Origin of moral virtues — habituation not nature
rubrics_metrics.description: Moral virtues do not come to us by nature nor against nature; we are equipped by nature with capacities but are perfected in virtues through custom/habituation (we become just by doing just acts).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasize repeated right actions and structured habituation (laws, upbringing, practice) to cultivate moral virtues; avoid expecting virtues as innate traits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acquisition principle: 'we become virtuous by doing virtuous acts'
rubrics_metrics.description: Virtues are produced by performing actions of the corresponding kind: builders become builders by building, harp-players by playing; similarly, by doing just acts we become just, by doing brave acts we become brave.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use practical exercises and role-specific practices to form character; laws and educational practices should create circumstances for appropriate action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lawmaking and education aim at habituation
rubrics_metrics.description: Law-givers and constitutions aim to make citizens good by habituation; the difference between good and bad constitutions lies partly in their success at forming correct habits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing political or educational systems, examine whether institutions foster the right habitual actions rather than merely teaching doctrines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Right Reason as the general maxim for action
rubrics_metrics.description: Acting 'in accordance with Right Reason' is the general maxim for moral action; particulars require practical judgement, as moral action lacks exactness and must be adapted to each case.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate actions by their conformity to right practical reasoning rather than rigid rules; recognize the role of phronesis (practical wisdom) to discern particulars.

rubrics_metrics.name: Doctrine of the mean — virtues spoiled by excess and defect
rubrics_metrics.description: Moral qualities are spoiled by both defect and excess (e.g., cowardice is excess of fearlessness? actually cowardice is excess of fear; rashness is deficiency), and virtue lies in due proportion between extremes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging character or behavior, look for the mean relative to the agent and circumstances; avoid one-size-fits-all prescriptions — the 'mean' is situational and determined by reason.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contextuality and non-exactness of moral judgement
rubrics_metrics.description: Matters of moral action and expediency lack fixed exactness: their application must be left to individual agents considering the exigencies of particular cases (as in medicine or navigation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess moral decisions with sensitivity to context, particulars, and professional judgment; penalize mechanical application of general rules when circumstances demand discretion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Psychology of the soul relevant to virtue
rubrics_metrics.description: The soul has Irrational and Rational parts; the irrational has a vegetative part and a desiring/appetitive part that can partake in reason. Moral virtue concerns the appetitive part being governed by reason.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In evaluating moral formation or actions, account for internal conflicts (desire vs reason) and the extent to which appetitive impulses are habituated to follow reason; use examples such as self-control vs weakness.
